862.title: Bhishma on kings: the fish and the mother
862.hook: a dying grandfather tells the new king that ruling well looks a lot like being pregnant
862.carry: rajadharma: power is for protecting the small
862.tomorrow: a famine and a starving sage: can dharma bend?
862.howItsDone: The Rajadharma section of the Shanti Parva is read by students of Indian political thought and by Hindu readers as teaching on just rule, and some teachers return to its pictures of the fish and the expectant mother.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-SIXTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday Shanti opened: Krishna stepped aside, parampara: wisdom handed down, person to person, and Bhishma, cleared of pain, began to teach.
screen: `SHANTI AND ANUSHASANA.` · `BHISHMA BEGINS.`

segments.voice: What is a king for? It sounds like a question for a political science class, but on the field it's urgent. Yudhishthira wears the crown now, and he still half wants to run. So he asks his grandfather plainly what a king's duties are. Bhishma's answer fills a long section of the Shanti Parva, known as Rajadharma, the dharma of kings. It's practical, sometimes blunt, full of advice about treasuries, spies and alliances. But a few pictures in it stick: a pond full of fish, and a mother carrying a child.
screen: `WHAT IS A KING FOR?` → `RAJADHARMA.` → `FISH, AND A MOTHER.`

segments.voice: First, the fish. Bhishma describes what happens when no one keeps order. The strong devour the weak, he says, the way big fish eat the little ones in the water. The weak need someone standing between them and the strong, and in Bhishma's teaching, that's the job: protection before glory. Second, the mother. A king, Bhishma says, should act like an expectant mother. A woman carrying a child, in his picture, sets aside some of what she'd like for herself, for the good of the child. So a king sets aside his own likes for the good of his people. It's a striking image from a warrior who vowed never to marry or have children. The ruler isn't the one being served. He's the one carrying. Underneath runs a warning: be gentle without being weak, and firm without being cruel. A king who is always soft gets ignored; one who is always harsh gets feared and hated. This is rajadharma, and it says something deep in Hindu teaching: power is itself a dharma, a duty that comes with the role, not a prize for winning. Yudhishthira wanted the forest. He's being told that carrying the throne can be its own self-denial. And the question reaches anyone handed a little power: a captain's armband, a team to run, a younger cousin for the weekend. Bhishma wouldn't ask what you get to decide. He'd ask: who is the small fish here, and are you standing in front of them?
screen: `BIG FISH EAT THE SMALL` · `PROTECTION BEFORE GLORY` · `A KING LIKE AN EXPECTANT MOTHER` · then, large: `POWER IS A DUTY, NOT A PRIZE`

segments.voice: Rest one hand lightly over your belly and bring to mind the people who depend on you, at home, at work, anywhere, and one thing you already set aside for their sake. Then think of one person who is the small fish somewhere in your world, and simply hold them in mind; if you pray, you can hold them in your prayer.
Rajadharma. The dharma of kings: protect the small fish, and carry your people the way a mother carries a child.

863.title: Vishvamitra and the forbidden food
863.hook: in a famine, a great sage creeps into a hut at night to steal a piece of dog meat, and gets caught
863.carry: apaddharma: dharma bends to save a life
863.tomorrow: a hunter shelters under a pigeon's tree. what is a guest owed?
863.howItsDone: Hindu teachers and writers on dharma discuss Apaddharma, the conduct allowed in real distress, and the story of Vishvamitra and the dog meat is told as a hard example of it.

segments.voice: Yudhishthira asks a hard question. What happens to dharma when everything falls apart? When there's war, famine, collapse, and the normal rules can't be kept? Bhishma's answer is a whole section called Apaddharma, dharma in times of distress. To explain it, he tells a story that's uncomfortable on purpose. A great sage, Vishvamitra, is starving. The rains have failed for a long time. The fields are dust, the villages empty, and people eat whatever they can find. One night, half dead, Vishvamitra slips into a poor hamlet looking for food.
screen: `WHEN THE RULES RUN OUT.` → `APADDHARMA.` → `A STARVING SAGE AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: In one hut he sees the haunch of a dog hanging. By the rules of his world, it's deeply forbidden food for a man like him. He decides to take it anyway. But the man who lives there wakes and catches him, and what follows isn't a fight. It's a debate. The householder, a man the society of that time placed at the bottom, argues for the rules. You're a sage, he says. You know dharma. Don't do this. Vishvamitra argues back. Staying alive comes first, because only the living can practice dharma at all. When I'm through this, I'll make amends with austerity. A dead sage helps no one. The householder isn't fully convinced, but Vishvamitra takes the meat, and even now, the story says, he means to offer it to the gods before he eats. Then the god Indra sends rain. The great sage steals; the man at the bottom defends dharma; the story leaves the discomfort in place. Two Hindu teachings sit inside it. Apaddharma: in real distress, dharma bends to protect life. And prayashchitta: the amends you make afterward, which is why Vishvamitra speaks of austerity even with the meat in his hand. But Bhishma warns this is for real distress, not convenience. A king who calls every inconvenience a famine has missed the lesson. You can still see this in Hindu homes. Many teachers say the sick and the very old may eat on a fast day, or keep a lighter fast with fruit or milk. The fast serves life. It was never meant to cost one.
screen: `THE FORBIDDEN FOOD` · `THE HOUSEHOLDER ARGUES FOR THE RULES` · `"ONLY THE LIVING PRACTICE DHARMA"` · then, large: `DHARMA BENDS TO SAVE A LIFE`

segments.voice: Let your breath settle and bring to mind a time you bent one of your own rules because things were falling apart. Breathe in and remember what was at stake; breathe out and ask honestly, without judging yourself, whether it was a real emergency or just convenience, and whether anything still needs repairing. If you pray, you can bring it into your prayer.
Apaddharma. Dharma for times of distress: a starving sage who stole forbidden food, and the man who argued with him.

864.title: The pigeons and the hunter
864.hook: a hunter caught in a storm shelters under the tree where he just trapped a pigeon, and her mate decides he is a guest

864.tomorrow: a snake, Death and Time: who is really to blame?
864.howItsDone: Hindu teaching treats the guest, atithi, as someone to be honored, and a line from the Taittiriya Upanishad, 'atithi devo bhava', let the guest be as a god, names the same ideal; Bhishma's story of the pigeons is retold as an illustration.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-SIXTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday a starving sage took forbidden food in a real emergency. Your line was apaddharma, dharma bends to save a life.

segments.voice: A storm breaks over the forest. A hunter, a hard man who lives by trapping birds, is caught out in it, soaked and shaking with cold. In his cage is a female pigeon he caught that day. He crouches under a big tree for shelter, not knowing the tree is her home. Up in its branches her mate is grieving, wondering where she's gone. And from inside the cage, she can hear him. Yudhishthira had asked about a person who gives shelter to someone who asks for it. This is the story Bhishma tells.
screen: `A STORM IN THE FOREST.` → `A HUNTER UNDER THEIR TREE.` → `SHE HEARS HER MATE.`

segments.voice: The female pigeon calls up to her mate, and what she says is startling. Don't grieve for me. This man has come to our home, cold and hungry. He's our guest. Treat him as one. And the male pigeon does. He brings an ember and dry leaves and makes a fire so the hunter can warm himself. Then he realizes he has nothing to feed his guest. So he offers himself, and drops into the fire, so the hunter will have food. The hunter is undone. The man who caught birds for a living has just watched a bird give its life to feed him. He opens the cage and lets the female go. But she, grieving her mate, follows him into the fire, and the story says the two rise to heaven together, shining. The hunter throws away his nets and his cage and goes into the forest to live in austerity. The word underneath all this is atithi, the guest. An old Hindu teaching, from the Taittiriya Upanishad, says atithi devo bhava: let the guest be to you as a god. In Bhishma's telling, that reaches even the one who hurt you. It's why, in so many Hindu homes, a visitor is handed water before much else is said, and nobody leaves without being offered food. The story is extreme on purpose; Bhishma isn't asking anyone to leap into fires. He's showing how far the welcome reaches: all the way to the person who did you harm.
screen: `"HE IS OUR GUEST"` · `A FIRE FOR THE HUNTER` · `THE HUNTER LAYS DOWN HIS NETS` · then, large: `ATITHI DEVO BHAVA: THE GUEST IS AS GOD`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest open and bring to mind someone who will come through your door, or into your day, who isn't easy to welcome. Picture doing what so many Hindu homes do first: handing them a glass of water, offering a seat, giving them your full attention. If you pray, hold that person in your prayer; if you don't, simply hold them in mind with goodwill.

865.title: Gautami, the snake, Death and Time
865.hook: a hunter drags a snake to a grieving mother so she can watch it die, and she tells him to let it go
865.carry: karma is a long chain, and you're one link
865.tomorrow: the sun turns north. how will Bhishma choose to go?
865.howItsDone: The story of Gautami, the snake, Death and Time is retold by Hindu teachers when they speak of karma and of letting go of revenge, and it stands at the opening of the Anushasana Parva.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-SIXTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday a pigeon honored the hunter who trapped his mate. Your line was atithi devo bhava, the guest is as God.

segments.voice: After all of Bhishma's teaching, Yudhishthira is still stuck in the same place. I caused all this, he says. I'm the reason you're lying on those arrows. So when the Anushasana Parva opens, Bhishma answers with a story about blame. An old woman named Gautami finds her son dead. A snake has bitten him. A hunter, Arjunaka, catches the snake, ties it with a cord, and drags it to her. Tell me how to kill it, he says. Fire, or cut it to pieces? Either is fine with me.
screen: `"I CAUSED ALL THIS."` → `A BOY BITTEN BY A SNAKE.` → `"HOW SHALL I KILL IT?"`

segments.voice: Gautami says: let it go. Killing it won't bring my son back, and it won't make me any less sad. The hunter argues; surely the guilty should pay. Then the snake speaks up. Don't blame me. I didn't act on my own. Death sent me. And Death, Mrityu, appears. Don't blame me either. I was directed by Time. Then Time itself, Kala, arrives and says: none of us is the real cause. The boy's own past actions, his karma, brought him here. We were only the instruments. Gautami accepts it, and the hunter lets the snake go. Each link points at the next, and the chain ends not in a villain but in the long working of actions and their results. That's karma as this story sees it: not a scoreboard kept on one person, but a long chain of many actions, many hands, running back further than anyone can see. Now look at who's listening. Yudhishthira is sure he's the snake, that the deaths are on him alone. Bhishma is saying, gently, that you are one link in something much longer, and you are not the whole of it. This isn't permission to stop caring. It's a way out of the guilt that eats a person alive and helps nobody. And notice who sees it first. Not the warrior, not the king. A grieving old mother, with every reason to want revenge. When grief says it was all my fault, Bhishma's answer is gentler and harder: own your link honestly, and don't claim the whole chain.
screen: `"LET IT GO"` · `THE SNAKE, DEATH, AND TIME` · `KARMA: A LONG CHAIN` · then, large: `YOU ARE ONE LINK, NOT THE WHOLE OF IT`

segments.voice: Soften your jaw and bring to mind something you still blame yourself for, and look honestly at your part in it. Then, breath by breath, let the other causes come into view, other people, timing, things nobody chose; you don't have to excuse anything, just let the picture be its true size. If you pray, you can bring that weight into your prayer.

segments.voice: Bhishma carries an unusual gift. Long ago, his father blessed him so that death would come only when he chose it. So he has been lying on the arrows, teaching, and waiting for a particular turning of the year: the time when the sun begins its northward course, called uttarayana, which the tradition holds as an auspicious time to die. He sent Yudhishthira back to the city to rule. Now the season has turned, and Yudhishthira returns to the field with fire, garlands and everything needed for the last rites.
screen: `DEATH ONLY WHEN HE CHOOSES.` → `WAITING FOR THE SUN TO TURN.` → `YUDHISHTHIRA RETURNS.`

segments.voice: Bhishma opens his eyes and sees them all around him: Yudhishthira and his brothers, the blind king Dhritarashtra, Gandhari, Kunti, Krishna. The time has come, he says. Then he turns to Krishna and asks for leave to go. A man who can choose his own death still asks permission to take it. Krishna gives it. And Bhishma does something the text describes almost like a meditation. He draws his life breath inward, part by part, and as it withdraws from each limb, the arrows there fall away and the wound closes. At last the breath leaves through the crown of his head, rising like a great light into the sky. Notice where his eyes are as he goes: on Krishna. That's a teaching Hindus still live by. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says whoever leaves the body remembering him comes to him, and the same chapter names the sun's northward months as the bright path. It was from this bed of arrows, the epic says, that Bhishma taught the Vishnu Sahasranama, the thousand names of Vishnu that many Hindus chant today. So at a Hindu deathbed, families often chant God's name, and place a drop of Ganga water or a tulsi leaf on the lips. Death isn't hidden or hurried. The last breath is given a direction. Then come the rites, and the river goddess Ganga rising from the water, weeping for her son, and Krishna comforting her: he has gone to the heavens. Don't grieve.

867.howItsDone: The Ashvamedhika Parva is the book of the Mahabharata that follows Bhishma's teachings; Hindus hear it in recitations of the full epic, and the horse sacrifice is remembered as a great royal rite of the Vedic world.

segments.voice: The water offerings for Bhishma have been poured into the Ganga. The great teacher is gone. Yudhishthira has listened to him at length, about kingship, duty and peace. He has the crown and the kingdom. And at the riverbank, in Ganguli's telling, he simply goes down, collapsing on the bank, overwhelmed by grief. Bhima holds him. Krishna speaks to him. And the old blind king Dhritarashtra, whose own sons died in this war, is the one who tells him to get up. A new book opens with a king on the ground.
screen: `THE OFFERINGS ARE POURED.` → `THE KING FALLS ON THE BANK.` → `THE BLIND KING SAYS: GET UP.`

segments.voice: Ashvamedhika is the book of the ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice: a great royal rite in which a consecrated horse wanders free, guarded by warriors. The idea isn't Yudhishthira's. He wants to leave the throne for the forest. It's the sage Vyasa who tells him grief can't be the whole of a king's life. Perform sacrifices, Vyasa says, give gifts, take up your work; the horse sacrifice will cleanse what weighs on you. Yudhishthira's answer is practical. The war has emptied the treasury, and he will not squeeze grieving people for more. So Vyasa points to old King Marutta, whose sacrifice in the Himalayas was so lavish that the gold left behind is still there. Go and bring it. Here's the Hindu shape underneath. Grief is given real room: the water offerings, the days of rites, the family sitting together. But it has a shape and an end. Many Hindu families keep ten to thirteen days of mourning after a death, closed with a ceremony, and then the household goes back to its work, its pujas, its festivals. The return isn't forgetting. It's dharma calling the living back up, and it often begins, as Vyasa says, with giving: feeding guests and priests, gifts in the name of the one who died. The book of the horse begins on the ground, with a blind king who lost every son telling the winner to stand.

If you pray, light a small lamp or offer it in their name; if you don't, simply hold them in mind as you do it.

868.title: Arjuna forgets the Gita
868.hook: after the war, in a quiet palace hall, Arjuna admits to Krishna that he has forgotten the teaching he heard on the battlefield

868.howItsDone: The Anugita is read by students of the Mahabharata alongside the Bhagavad Gita, and commentators and teachers in several Hindu traditions have discussed how the two teachings relate.

segments.voice: Yesterday Ashvamedhika opened with Yudhishthira on the riverbank and Vyasa pointing to old King Marutta's gold. Your line was mourning has its days; then dharma calls you up.
screen: `ASHVAMEDHIKA.` · `MARUTTA'S GOLD.`

segments.voice: I've forgotten it. That, in plain terms, is what Arjuna tells Krishna. The war is over. The two friends are walking in the great assembly hall the Pandavas have won back, with time on their hands at last. And Arjuna brings up the conversation in the chariot, between the two armies, before the fighting began: the teaching people now call the Bhagavad Gita. What you told me then, he says, has slipped from my mind. Please tell it to me again.
screen: `THE WAR IS OVER.` → `A WALK IN THE HALL.` → `"I'VE FORGOTTEN IT."`

segments.voice: Krishna doesn't pretend that's fine. In Ganguli's telling he's displeased. You didn't hold on to what I told you in confidence, he says, and I'm sorry you forgot it. Then something surprising: he can't simply repeat it. He spoke on the battlefield, he explains, while united in yoga, and he can't call it back word for word. So instead he tells Arjuna an old story. A brahmana meets a perfected sage, a siddha, and asks the big questions: how a living being dies, how it is born again, what binds it to action, and how it goes free. More old dialogues follow. Together these chapters are known as the Anugita. They return to the Gita's ground, the self, action and freedom, but in a new shape: no army, no chariot, just questions asked in peace. Even Arjuna, who heard the Gita face to face, lost hold of it once the crisis passed. Insight doesn't keep by itself. This is why Hindus don't read the Gita once and shelve it. The practice is called svadhyaya, one's own study: coming back to sacred words again and again. Many families read a chapter a day; some learn a verse a week; some gather to chant the whole Gita on Gita Jayanti. Not because they've never heard it. Because, like Arjuna, they know it slips. Krishna doesn't hand Arjuna the old words. He sits down in the hall and starts again.

segments.voice: If you have a Gita or another sacred book at home, open it anywhere and read one verse slowly, twice. If not, bring back one line from these lessons.
